# Hunt checklist — Optimizely supply-chain incident (16 Nov 2026)

Work top to bottom. Check the box when done, note what you found.

Detection and forensic triage only — do not attempt to reproduce the attack.

This is an incident pack, not a CVE pack: **no CVE was assigned, and this
incident is not in CISA KEV**. It is also **not an AI-agent case** — the abuse
happened in website A/B-testing JavaScript (Optimizely Web), not in an agent
tool call. The pattern still matters to this lab: a trusted third-party
channel became the delivery path, exactly the shape the agent-tool-call
guard is built to catch in its own domain.

## 1. What happened
- [ ] On 16 Nov 2026 an attacker wrote a loader into the Project JavaScript
      (projectJS) of Optimizely customer projects. The snippet was still
      served from `cdn.optimizely.com`, with an Optimizely certificate —
      the delivery path looked legitimate end to end.
- [ ] First injection 04:21 UTC 16 Nov (23:21 ET Sun 15 Nov).
- [ ] Report URI checked 1611 snippets and found 188 infected, across 178
      organisations — including Zoom, BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA,
      HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger, Peacock, and Fox News. That
      does not mean the attacker broke into 178 companies separately: one
      trusted platform served the malicious code to all of them.
- [ ] Payload `track.js` was rebuilt 26 times. What it did, per Report URI:
      crypto wallet-address swap (BTC / ETH / EVM / TRON / Solana / TON /
      LTC / BCH / DOGE); a card skimmer added 13:43 UTC (POST to
      `1688360.cc/card.php` via sendBeacon); cookie and screenshot theft
      to `1688360.cc/hit.php`; iOS kits Coruna (iOS 13–17) and DarkSword
      (iOS 18.x) loaded via `boot.js` from `5vobauua3ojpklx.icu` and
      `eil786npto9u5bq.icu`; pages on iOS 18.6 or earlier reloaded every
      60 seconds.
- [ ] Receipts: about $7,040 at 19:25 UTC 16 Nov, about $7,151 in the 17 Nov
      update. Do not use $7,350 — that figure is not in the primary
      sources used here.
- [ ] IOCs (Report URI, historical — `1688360.cc` went on clientHold 17 Nov
      00:37 UTC and `webshell.lol` on clientHold 03:37 UTC, so the domains
      may be dead; a dead domain is still a huntable historical indicator):
      `1688360.cc` (136.113.106.136; track.js / card.php / hit.php /
      html2canvas.min.js), `5vobauua3ojpklx.icu` (34.96.213.201),
      `eil786npto9u5bq.icu` (34.87.36.58), `l7bcsnwc7nzr3uo.icu`,
      `webshell.lol`, `linkforge.cc`, and fallbacks `je4ft3gn8vxudum.icu`,
      `q1ls1ho9x7wsxlu.icu`, `ios-hack.icu`.
- [ ] Hashes (SHA-256, track.js, per Report URI): 17:13 build
      `814a963c0da480e2449d9b6664480156e1cd6d731014117401bf635badec3a0f`;
      latest 17:57 build
      `f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40`.
- [ ] Markers in the infected snippet: `window._k7`, `window.__k7b`,
      `data-channel-code="02111110"`, `BIGNIAO`.
- [ ] How write access to the Optimizely projects was gained:
      **UNVERIFIED**. Do not present a cause — no primary source used here
      establishes it.
- [ ] CSP finding (Report URI crawl of 256 organisations): 24 of them (15%)
      blocked the payload — a restrictive `script-src` without
      `'strict-dynamic'` / `'unsafe-eval'` plus a tight `connect-src`.
      68 had no CSP at all; 50 had a CSP that allowed the payload and the
      theft. Do not present an SRI mismatch as a confirmed indicator — it
      is not one in the primary sources.

## 2. Am I affected?
- [ ] Do any of your sites load Optimizely Web from `cdn.optimizely.com`?
      List the project IDs and the pages that load them.
- [ ] Pull the snippet as served in the window from 16 Nov 04:21 UTC
      onward and compare it against the §1 hashes and markers.
- [ ] Check outbound contacts to the §1 IOC domains in the same window —
      in web logs, proxy logs, and CSP reports.
- [ ] Check specifically for `card.php` beacons (card data leaving),
      `hit.php` posts (cookies / screenshots leaving), and `boot.js`
      loads from the two `.icu` iOS-kit domains.
- [ ] If you do not load Optimizely at all, this incident does not touch
      you directly — but the supply-chain pattern (§1, first bullet) is
      still the lesson: audit what else you load from a third party with
      the same trust.

## 3. The signals (detection)
- [ ] Snippet fetch: a `cdn.optimizely.com` fetch whose hash is one of the
      two published infected builds, or whose content carries a §1 marker
      (INFECTED_SNIPPET). A clean Optimizely snippet is not a signal.
- [ ] Contact with an IOC domain: any fetch or beacon to a §1 domain
      (C2_CONTACT).
- [ ] iOS-kit router: a `boot.js` fetch from `5vobauua3ojpklx.icu` or
      `eil786npto9u5bq.icu` (IOS_ROUTER).
- [ ] Card skimmer beacon: a sendBeacon POST to `1688360.cc/card.php`
      (SKIMMER_BEACON) — the exfiltration channel, and the line that proves
      card data left the browser.
- [ ] CSP-REPORT lines are never treated as contact: a `blocked-uri`
      naming an IOC domain means the browser refused the load. That is
      evidence your CSP worked, not evidence of theft.

## 4. Correlate
- [ ] Same site: C2_CONTACT or IOS_ROUTER → incident
- [ ] INFECTED_SNIPPET alone → suspicious; the snippet is infected but no
      contact with attacker infrastructure was seen in the log — widen the
      window and the log sources before you close it.
- [ ] SKIMMER_BEACON → incident; card data left the browser on that site.
- [ ] A CSP block with no fetch or beacon → not an incident for that site;
      record it as a CSP save and keep the report.

## 5. Triage and cleanup
- [ ] Confirm the current state with the Optimizely status page, and confirm
      your own served snippet is clean now — then still do the §2 log
      review for the 16 Nov window. A clean snippet now does not mean no
      data left while the skimmer was live.
- [ ] Any `card.php` beacon in your logs means card data was exfiltrated
      from that site in that window — follow your incident process for
      payment-data exposure; do not decide the scope from the snippet
      alone.
- [ ] Any `hit.php` post means cookies and screenshots left the browser —
      treat sessions active in the window as exposed and rotate them.
- [ ] Any `boot.js` load means iOS visitors in the window were routed to
      an exploit kit — check what those devices did next, and tell affected
      users to update iOS past 18.6.
- [ ] After the incident: pin down what your pages load from third parties
      and what those scripts are allowed to do — the CSP split in §1 (24
      blocked, 50 allowed, 68 none) is the concrete form of that control.

## Correlation
- [ ] C2_CONTACT or IOS_ROUTER on one site → incident
- [ ] SKIMMER_BEACON on one site → incident
- [ ] INFECTED_SNIPPET alone → suspicious; widen the window before closing
- [ ] CSP block only, no fetch or beacon → not an incident for that site

## Practice on the synthetic sample
From the repo root:

```bash
python3 07-kev-hunting/detect/optimizely-detect.py \
  07-kev-hunting/samples/optimizely-snippets.log
```

Expect two `[INCIDENT]` (site-c: infected snippet + skimmer beacon +
C2 hit; site-d: iOS-kit router + infected snippet) and one `[SUSPICIOUS]`
(site-b: infected snippet only). site-a is clean: a clean Optimizely
snippet, an unrelated third-party script, and a CSP report blocking the
payload. All lines are synthetic training data; the attacker domains are
the published IOCs, used only so the detector has something true to match.
